sources.citation: Schapper, Antoinette & Erik Zobel. 2024. The classification of Irarutu and Koiwai: A new proposal. Oceanic Linguistics 63(2): 338-366. doi:10.1353/ol.2024.a946248 (HAL deposit hal-05661108).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 3.1 is historical phonology only. p.350: 'The fact that vowels in different syllables are retained in Koiwai and Irarutu indicates that stress did not always fall on the same syllable in their immediate ancestor.. The different patterns of vowel loss suggest that the stress system of the immediate ancestor of Koiwai and Irarutu was not entirely predictable.' No synchronic statement of where Koiwai word stress falls. Koiwai data taken from Walker 1990 (Toolbox lexicon) and Walker 1980 'Notes on Kowiai grammar' (unpublished MS).

sources.citation: Greenhill, Blust & Gray (eds.), Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database, list 161 'Koiwai (Irian Jaya)', source Roland Walker (SIL), personal communication 2005.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No prose statement; but 118 of 228 forms carry an acute accent (Walker's stress marking). Crude count: accent on penultimate vowel ~95 forms (mafína, namáta, afúna, tóron), on final vowel ~19 (marír, timét, barém, tanóm, lafé, iná), earlier ~4. Data only — suggests predominantly penultimate but lexically variable stress.

One paragraph (p.87) compares Koiwai and Malay phonology (bilabial allophones of /f/; Namatota dialect lost prenasalised voiced stops, retained in Kayumerah and Adijaya dialects).
